passage:
Rafiq: Did you use the lab manual I gave you?
Anjali: Yes, thanks again, it really helped.
Rafiq: Good. Btw saw you at the canteen with Mehul's group, not with us.
Anjali: Just had tea there.
Rafiq: Ok. Just saying, I've done a lot for you this sem.
Anjali: I know. I'm grateful.
Rafiq: So you're coming for the fest committee thing on Sunday na?
Anjali: I have my cousin's engagement on Sunday.
Rafiq: Hmm. After the manual, the notes, the cycle... thought you'd make time.
Anjali typed "sorry", deleted it, typed it again, deleted it again. She looked at the borrowed manual on her shelf. Then she wrote: "I'll return the manual and the cycle tomorrow. Thank you for all of it. I can't come on Sunday."
Rafiq: ?

qa.q: What event does Anjali have on Sunday?
qa.a: She has her cousin's engagement on Sunday.

qa.q: What was Anjali feeling when she kept typing and deleting "sorry"?
qa.a: She felt torn and guilty, obliged because of all the help, yet uneasy about being watched and pushed.

qa.q: What small step helped Anjali keep her dignity?
qa.a: Returning the manual and the cycle with a clear thank-you and a plain no let her close the debt without apologising for her own plans.

qa.q: How might Rafiq see his own help?
qa.a: He may see it as kindness that earns loyalty in return, without noticing that the hidden expectation makes Anjali feel watched.

grounding: Shows a student who accepted a senior's help beginning to feel obliged and watched because the help came with hidden expectations.

passage: The first monsoon storm in Kalna flooded Damini's rented room ankle-deep, and her lesson registers floated against the cot. By evening Bidisha from next door stood at the door with a steel tiffin of rice and fish curry and two dry saris over her arm. Damini's words came out in a rush: "Oh no, you shouldn't have, I'm such a burden, I'm so sorry, I'll pay you back somehow—" She stopped. Bidisha's face had gone a little flat. Damini took a breath, took the tiffin with both hands, and said, "Thank you. I was really hungry." Bidisha brightened at once. She spread the registers on her own verandah to dry, told Damini exactly which pages to press flat under the brick, and stayed to watch her eat.

qa.q: What did Bidisha bring in the steel tiffin?
qa.a: She brought rice and fish curry.

qa.q: Why did Damini's first words come out as a rush of apologies?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and guilty about needing help, as if being helped made her a burden.

qa.q: Which reply worked better, and why?
qa.a: The simple "Thank you. I was really hungry." worked better, because it let Bidisha's kindness land instead of turning it into a debt 🙂

qa.q: How did Bidisha seem to feel when Damini just said thank you?
qa.a: She brightened and seemed pleased to be useful, drying the registers and staying to watch Damini eat.

grounding: Shows a young teacher switching from anxious apology to a simple thank-you, which lets her neighbour feel useful.

passage:
Joseph read the message twice before he answered.
Siddharth: bro, one more favour. Can you lend me something for a new phone? Mine's cracked
Joseph: Sid, I can't this month.
Siddharth: Come on, you just got your increment 😅
Joseph: I did. A big part goes home for Chechi's college fees, and I've kept aside what I need to get through the month.
Siddharth: So you're saying no.
Joseph: I'm saying no to money. Not to you. I'll come on Saturday and help you fix your CV for the bank job, and I know a repair shop that can change the screen.
Siddharth: ...ok fine. Sorry, I've asked a lot lately.
Joseph: You have 🙂 But I'd rather say no now than start avoiding your calls.
Siddharth: Fair. Saturday, 5?
Joseph: Saturday, 5. Bring the phone.

qa.q: What will Joseph help Siddharth with on Saturday?
qa.a: He will help Siddharth fix his CV for the bank job, and Siddharth is to bring the phone.

qa.q: What does Joseph's line about avoiding calls suggest he is worried about?
qa.a: He is worried that giving past his limit would turn into resentment and make him avoid his friend, which he fears more than saying no.

qa.q: What worked in the way Joseph said no?
qa.a: He was clear about the limit, gave a short reason without over-explaining, and offered help he could truly give, like the CV and the repair shop.

qa.q: How did Siddharth take the refusal?
qa.a: He pushed a little at first, then apologised for asking a lot and fixed a time, so the friendship stayed intact.

grounding: Shows a young earner who supports his family setting a clear limit with a friend so that giving does not turn into resentment.

passage: By nine at night there was a queue outside Keerthana's door in the girls' hostel, even if nobody called it that. Pooja needed her chemistry notes photographed. Her roommate wanted to cry about a fight with her mother, again. Then a message from Mohit in the class group: "Keerthana you have the physics answers na? Send pls 🙏" She sent them. She always did. Afterwards she sat on her bed with her own homework untouched and noticed that her jaw was tight. When Pooja knocked again, "Just one tiny thing," Keerthana heard herself say "Sure!" in her brightest voice, then shut the door and stared at the wall. Nobody had asked how her day was. She realised nobody ever did, and that she had never given them a reason to.

qa.q: What did Mohit ask for in the class group?
qa.a: He asked for the physics answers.

qa.q: What was Keerthana feeling as she sat with her own homework untouched?
qa.a: She felt drained and quietly resentful; her jaw was tight even though she kept saying yes.

qa.q: What small step could Keerthana try tomorrow?
qa.a: She could tell Pooja, "Not tonight, I need to do my own work," and share notes at one set time instead of whenever someone asks.

qa.q: How might Pooja see Keerthana?
qa.a: Pooja probably sees her as the cheerful one who never minds, because the bright "Sure!" hides how tired she is.

grounding: Shows a teenager whom everyone relies on for notes, comfort and favours starting to feel drained and resentful in that role.

passage:
College counselling centre, session note, Friday.
Ramesh came in about poor sleep, but his phone buzzed four times during the hour. Each time it was Eshaan. This week Ramesh has taken late-night calls from three friends about a breakup, marks and a fight at home, most nights until two. Tonight Eshaan wants to talk again about an argument in their project group. Ramesh said, "If I don't pick up, I'm a selfish person." His hands were shaking a little. I asked when he had last said no to anyone. He could not remember. We practised one line: "I care, and I can't talk tonight. Tomorrow at lunch?" He sent it while still in the room, then sat with his eyes shut. Eshaan replied: "ok, lunch 👍". Follow-up next Friday.

qa.q: How many times did Ramesh's phone buzz during the hour?
qa.a: It buzzed four times.

qa.q: What was Ramesh feeling when he said he would be a selfish person?
qa.a: He felt guilty and anxious, his hands shaking a little, as if saying no would be a real wrong.

qa.q: Why did the practised line help?
qa.a: It kept the care and offered a clear time, so Ramesh could rest tonight without dropping his friend 👍

qa.q: How did Eshaan respond to the message, and what does it show?
qa.a: Eshaan simply agreed to lunch, which shows the no did not hurt the friendship the way Ramesh feared.

grounding: Shows a student worn out from listening to friends all week feeling guilty about declining a call, and a counsellor helping him say no kindly.

passage:
14 March, 11:40 pm
Divyansh's diary, since nobody else is listening today. Paid the electricity bill on the way home, picked up Papa's medicines, then Mummy called: Siddharth needs his laptop fee by Monday, and "you're the eldest, beta." I said yes before she finished. I always do. At dinner everyone talked about Siddharth's college fest. I nodded off sitting up and Papa laughed, "Office has made you lazy." I wanted to say I've been going since seven. I didn't. I do love them. I chose this. But tonight I'd give anything for one person to ask if I'm tired. Maybe I'll tell Siddharth tomorrow. He's the one who might actually hear it.

qa.q: What did Papa say when Divyansh nodded off at dinner?
qa.a: He laughed and said, "Office has made you lazy."

qa.q: What was Divyansh feeling at the end of the day?
qa.a: Divyansh felt exhausted and unseen, still loving the family but longing for one person to ask about being tired.

qa.q: What could Divyansh say to Siddharth tomorrow?
qa.a: Divyansh could say plainly, "I've been running on empty. Can you take one errand this week?", which asks for help without blaming anyone.

qa.q: How might Papa see Divyansh nodding off at dinner?
qa.a: Papa sees only a sleepy Divyansh and turns it into a joke, not knowing the day began at seven with bills and errands.

grounding: Shows an eldest child who gives willingly to the family feeling exhausted and unseen when nobody notices the cost.

passage: So there's this guy in my flat, Varun. I'm Swati, I've shared the flat with him and two others for three years, and Varun is the one who fixes everything. Wi-Fi, the landlord, someone's breakup, he's there. Last month I started noticing things. He stopped cooking on Sundays. He answered in one word. When Nikita asked him to look at her bike, he snapped, "Can someone else do it for once?" and went to his room. We all went quiet. My first thought was, rude. Then I thought, when did any of us last ask him anything? So I knocked. I said, "I'm doing your laundry this week and I'm making dinner on Sunday. Don't argue." He just stood in the doorway for a bit. Then he said, "Okay." That's it. Okay. But he ate two plates.

qa.q: What did Varun snap when Nikita asked about her bike?
qa.a: He snapped, "Can someone else do it for once?"

qa.q: What was Swati feeling after Varun snapped?
qa.a: Swati first felt annoyed and thought he was rude, then felt a guilty jolt, realising none of them had asked about Varun in a long time 😔

qa.q: What made Swati's offer work?
qa.a: It was concrete, laundry and Sunday dinner, and it didn't make Varun explain or ask, so he could simply accept.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Varun when Swati knocked?
qa.a: He was probably surprised and moved, since he stood in the doorway quietly before accepting, and being looked after was new for him.

grounding: Shows a flatmate noticing that the usual helper has turned curt and withdrawn, and offering to look after him for a change.

passage:
"Pankaj, the society secretary called again. They want you for the Diwali committee."
"I'm saying no this year, Vidya."
"You? You've run it four years."
"And by every Thursday I've been snapping at the kids. Look." He turned the wall calendar toward her. Every Sunday morning had a green circle. "That's mine. No calls, no errands."
"And Appa's clinic visits?"
"Ravi takes the first and third Saturday. I asked him yesterday. He said he'd been waiting for me to ask."
Vidya laughed. "Who are you, and what have you done with my husband?"
"Still him. Just one who wants to stay nice past Thursday."
His phone buzzed. The secretary. He picked up. "Namaste ji. Thank you for thinking of me. This year I can't, but I'll hand over the vendor list by Friday."

qa.q: Who will take Appa to the clinic on the first and third Saturday?
qa.a: Ravi will take him.

qa.q: What does Pankaj's comment about snapping at the kids suggest he felt before?
qa.a: It suggests he felt worn out and irritable from giving so much, and worried that his kindness was turning into short temper.

qa.q: Which of Pankaj's changes seems most useful, and why?
qa.a: Asking Ravi to share the clinic visits helps most, because it spreads a regular load instead of only resting once.

qa.q: How might Ravi feel about being asked?
qa.a: Ravi seems glad, even relieved, since he said he had been waiting to be asked.

grounding: Shows a person who gives a lot scheduling rest, sharing a family load and saying a clear, polite no to one request.

passage: After old Hariram from the next lane was cremated, Charu sat on the edge of the village well, swinging her legs and watching the smoke thin out over the fields. Her cousin Trisha sat beside her. "Didi, why do people die?" "Bodies get very old or very sick, and then they stop working," Trisha said. "It happens to every living thing." Charu frowned. "Then why are we even here?" "I don't fully know. Some people say it's to love each other and do good work. What do you think?" "To look after the goats," Charu said seriously. "And what happens after?" "Families believe different things. Nobody knows for sure. Dadi believes he has gone to God." Charu nodded and held Trisha's hand all the way home.

qa.q: Where did Charu sit after the cremation?
qa.a: She sat on the edge of the village well, swinging her legs.

qa.q: What might Charu have been feeling when she asked why people die?
qa.a: She was probably curious and a little unsettled after the cremation, trying to make sense of death.

qa.q: What made Trisha's answers helpful?
qa.a: They were honest and simple, she admitted what she didn't know, and she asked what Charu thought instead of changing the subject.

qa.q: What would change if Trisha had said, "You're too small for such questions"?
qa.a: Charu might feel her questions were wrong and keep her worries to herself, instead of feeling close enough to hold Trisha's hand all the way home.

grounding: Shows a child asking why people die, why we are here and what comes next, and an older cousin answering honestly and simply.

passage:
Dear Mohit Bhaiya,
You asked on the phone why I sound "different every month". Fair question. In June I joined the lake clean-up group and wanted to be a marine biologist. In July I cut my hair short and wore only black. In August I went to the gurdwara with Harleen every morning just to sit in the quiet, even though our family isn't Sikh, and it felt more like home than almost anything. In September I left the quiz club because they only talk about ranks. Mummy calls it phases. Maybe. But each one told me something. The lake felt useful. The quiet felt true. The black clothes felt like a costume. I'm keeping two out of four, which honestly isn't bad.
Please don't laugh. I'm trying to find what's worth caring about, and I'm serious about it even if it looks messy.
Minakshi

qa.q: Where did Minakshi go every morning in August?
qa.a: Minakshi went to the gurdwara with Harleen, just to sit in the quiet.

qa.q: How does Minakshi feel about being called "different every month"?
qa.a: Minakshi feels a little defensive and worried about being laughed at, but also serious and hopeful about the search.

qa.q: How could Mohit reply in a way that helps?
qa.a: Mohit could skip the jokes and ask which of the two kept things feels most alive, taking the search as seriously as Minakshi does.

qa.q: How might Mummy's view of these changes differ from Minakshi's?
qa.a: Mummy sees phases that look random from outside, while for Minakshi each one is a careful test of what matters.

grounding: Shows a teenager trying out a cause, a faith space, a style and a group in a serious search for what feels worth caring about.
